lesson.title: Symmetric, Skewed, or Something Else: Describing Shape
lesson.summary: The shape of a distribution, whether symmetric or skewed, unimodal or multimodal, determines how the mean and median relate to each other and which summary statistics are appropriate to use.
lesson.body:
Once a distribution has been displayed, whether through a dotplot, stemplot, or histogram, describing its shape is one of the first and most important steps in understanding what the data are telling you. Shape refers to the overall pattern the values form: whether the distribution is symmetric, with the left and right sides mirroring each other, or skewed, with one side stretched out into a longer tail than the other, and whether the data pile up around a single peak, called unimodal, around two distinct peaks, called bimodal, or show no clear peak at all, called roughly uniform.

Skewness describes the direction of the longer tail, and the naming convention follows the tail, not the hump where most of the data sit. A distribution is skewed right, or positively skewed, when it has a long tail stretching toward larger values, even though most of the data cluster on the smaller side, a common pattern for variables like income or house prices, where most values are modest but a few very large values stretch the tail out. A distribution is skewed left, or negatively skewed, when the long tail stretches toward smaller values instead, with most data clustered on the larger side.

Shape has a direct, useful connection to the relationship between the mean and the median of a distribution. In a distribution that is skewed right, the long tail of unusually large values pulls the mean upward more than it pulls the median, so typically the mean ends up larger than the median. In a distribution skewed left, the reverse happens, and the mean typically ends up smaller than the median. In a perfectly symmetric distribution, the mean and median are equal.

Consider ten employees' one way commute times in minutes: 10, 12, 12, 13, 15, 15, 16, 18, 20, and 45, where one employee has an unusually long commute. The mean is found by adding all ten values and dividing by 10: 10 plus 12 plus 12 plus 13 plus 15 plus 15 plus 16 plus 18 plus 20 plus 45 equals 176, and 176 divided by 10 equals 17.6 minutes. The median, since the data are already sorted and there are 10 values, is the average of the 5th and 6th values, both 15, giving a median of 15 minutes. The mean, 17.6, is noticeably larger than the median, 15, exactly the pattern expected for a right skewed distribution, since the single long commute of 45 minutes pulls the mean upward while the median, which only depends on the position of values rather than their exact size, stays anchored near where most of the data actually sit.

Describing shape well means going beyond a single label. A complete description typically covers whether the distribution is roughly symmetric or skewed and in which direction, how many peaks or modes it has, and whether any individual values stand apart from the rest as unusual, sometimes called outliers, such as the 45 minute commute in the example above. Learning to read shape directly from a dotplot, stemplot, or histogram, rather than only from calculated numbers, is a skill that pays off throughout the rest of statistics, since the shape of a distribution often determines which summary statistics and which statistical methods are appropriate to use on it later in the course.
